content: Collision programming involves [b]two[/b] stages:
Given two moving entities with a given shape or bounds, determine if they intersect. Detection is a geometric problem.
When two entities collide, determine what to do to 'resolve' the physics of the simulation.

In the real world, objects can have arbitrary shapes or interaction surfaces. In programming, these are difficult to store, compute, and simulate accurately. All shapes in computer simulations must be made of [b]primitive[/b] types:
2D: Line, Triangle, Circle, Rectangle
3D: Sphere, Plane, Cylinder, Prism
Using these types we define the concept of a [b]Bounding Shape[/b] - a simple shape that simulates the interactions bounds of a complex one.

image.caption: Complex shapes with simple bounding shapes.

content: The simplest 2d bounding shape to store and compute is a circle with a given radius.
Other 2d bounding shapes can be constructed in a number of line segments. The simplest of these is a rectangle.

Most classic 2D games use rectangular sprite graphics. These rectangular images make a natural fit for a rectangular bounding box. Usually the bounding box will be the smallest rectangle that can fit the sprite.

image.caption: A variety of sprites and their bounding boxes.
A few sprites whose bounding boxes are defined in a custom size.

content: Rectangles in a 2D plane can take any orientation as long as all four corners form 90 degree angles. Detecting intersections of arbitrary rectangles can be quite slow, involving computing if all lines intersect. By aligning rectangles with the x/y axis, you can trade arbitrary alignment for vary fast intersection / collision checks.
The simplest collision check you can perform is to see if a single point is inside an AABB.

The next check is to determine if two AABBs intersect. Horizontal overlap happens if the top of each box is higher than the bottom of the other. Vertical overlap happens if the left of each box is less than the right of the other. Two AABBs intersect if they have both horizontal and vertical overlap. This does not tell us by how much they intersected.

image.caption: Logic for checking if a Point is inside an AABB.

content: Centered AABBs are AABBs that use the center of the Entity for the position of the AABB.The overalp betwen two Centered AABBs can be found by calculating the delta between the two center points and comparing it to the widths and heights of the AABBs

image.caption: Sample code for a Centered AABB.
Formula for finding the overlap between two Centered AABBs.

content: Collision resolution depends entirely on the physics of your game world; what should happen when two objects collide? In some cases, one of the objects should be pushed out to no overlap. In other cases, one object gets blown up.

When detecting collisions in the game, they will first happen in a specific frame. The frame before collision is detected, there will be no collision. When you detect overlap, you will want to know which direction movement came from. If you store the AABBs position in the previous frame, then you can check for horizontal or vertical overlap there. That will give you an indication from which direction movement came.

Fore example, if in the previous frame overlap.y > 0, then that means collision movement came from the left or right side. Resolve collision by pushing in an x direction. If in the previous frame overlap.x > 0, then that means collision movement came from the top or bottom. Resolve collision by pushing in an y direction.

compund_text: A collision came from the top if previous overlap.x > 0 and its y is higher.
A collision came from the bottom if previous overlap.x > 0 and its y is lower.

content: What if their was no overlap in either the x or y in the previous frame? You have to decide how to resolve collisions based on previous position and/or size.

content.caption: Collision between two objects that had no overlap in a previous frame.

content: What if an entity overlap with multiple entities, such as moving near a stack? Order of collision checks can help, but may be tricky.
All collision resolution discussed is for the simple case of avoiding overlap. This is useful for
walking on tiles
not being able to pass through tiles
bullets hitting entities
There are still other kinds of collision resolution:
Kinematic object elastic / inelastic collisions
Physics simulators with mass and force
Super Mario Bros collision detection operate by using simple AABB overlap detection. If Mario and an enemy collide, Mario kills them if he is moving downwards, ignoring and x overlap.

It could not:

The [b]Game[/b] class in Assignment 2 handled all the functionality for the game. Some of this functionality would be needed in all game scenes:

Some of this functionality should be specific to the type of game scene currently on display:

section.header: Assignment 3 Architecture - Game Engine and Scenes
content: In Assignment 3, we will split the previous [b]Game[/b] class into two separate classes to handle the functionality. The first is the [b]GameEngine[/b] class, responsible for functionality present in all scenes, constructing and management of scenes, and running or quitting the game. The other is the [b]Scene[/b] class, responsible for functionality specific to each scene and entities relevant to that scene.

The [b]GameEngine[/b] class will store top-level game data, such as assets, the game window, and scenes. It will perform top-level functionality, such as changing scenes and handling input. Its Run() method will contain the main game loop. And a pointer to the [b]GameEngine[/b] instance will be passed to all [b]Scenes[/b] in their constructor, giving them access to assets, the main window, and other game scenes.

Scene-derived classes will store scene-specific data, such as the level, a pointer to the player, or the config. Scene-specific Systems are defined within the derived class. Some Scene-derived classes will require very different functionality, so [i]update()[/i], [i]doAction()[/i], and [i]render()[/i] should be implemented for each scene.

In order to facilitate scene switching, the [b]GameEngine[/b] class will store a dictionary of identifiers pointing to [b]Scene[/b] instances. The current scene's identifier will be stored as a field. Method 'getCurrentScene()' will also return the active [b]Scene.changeScene(string, scene)[/b] changes the scene to a new scene, or a previously-stored scene. This mimics a finite state machine for [b]Scene[/b] switching.

content: Assets are loaded into an [b]Assets[/b] class where they can be referenced by name.
The [b]Assets[/b] class will store the assets in a dictionary.

The [b]Assets[/b] class will live inside the [b]GameEngine[/b] class, and will be initialized inside [b]GameEngine::init()[/b]. Scenes will access the assets library via pointers to the [b]GameEngine[/b] instance.

Assets should be loaded once at the beginning of the game, and are then available in any scene. For larger applications, you may want to load assets per scene. For example, loading screens on level change in most games are for Asset management and other data loading purposes.

A texture is a graphic mapped to a shape. It can be generate dynamically or loaded from an existing image file. A rectangular shaoe with a texture attached to it is typically called a [i]'Sprite'[/i]. Sprites are ver common in older games - some older computers had sprite hardware.
Sometimes the texture will not be the same size as the Entity's shape. You can specify a sub-rectangle of the texture which will be drawn.
Textures can be loaded from file in Godot:

Games have many textures that will be used, and it can be hard to manage files. Texture sheets can be used that store many tetxures within the same image. This is an easy way to organize and store textures. If the entire sheet is loaded into graphics memory, less texture swapping occurs.
Instead of loading a different texture for each character, pose, or tile, you just assign the correct sub-rectangle that is to be drawn. Rectangles can be stored as variables or computed dynamically.

content: Games are interactive and players get to influence gameplay via inout devices. Inputs are given by the player to influence what Entities do. The result of an input is usually an action the player wants to happen in the game, such as jumping, shooting, or moving. Actions can also be called commands.

How the player inputs the actions isn't important, as long as it is easy to perform. Similarly, the game engine shouldn't care which inout device caused an action to be triggered. The game engine should only care about the logic required to carry out the action. Ideally, you want to decouple the action logic from the inouts that triggered them.

In Assignment 2, actions were performed inside the event loop. When a specific key was pressed, specific game logic was called. You couldn't separate the two processes, or re-map keys for instance. All input handling and systems logic was done in the [b]Game[/b] class, since there was only one scene.

image.caption: A review of the Assignment 2 Architecture.

content: We want to implement a system in a scene where the scene only know the type of action the player wants to perform, and doesn't care about where the input came from. We will want an Action class that will be a container for the type of action the player wants the scene to perform. All user input will be handled within the [b]GameEngine[/b] class, where [b]Actions[/b] will be created and dispatched to scenes to have their logic carried out. The [b]Scene[/b] class will have a doAction() method that will perform logic based on a specific [b]Action[/b] object.

Actions will be given a name (usually associated with the action, such as jump or left). Actions initiated by keyboard or controller will have two phases: press and release which denote the start and end of an action. So Actions will have a type of action as well, [i]'START'[/i] or [i]'END'[/i].

image.caption: Sample implementation of the Action class.

content: Action Start = Press Button
Action End  = Release Button
For example:
Would be a command for the player to move right continuously as if the right input button were being held down. The action would only stop with:

We want to be able to map specific user input to a specific Action object. Key Input Events are usually mapped to Integer constants. You could use a dictionary for that. The Scene base class will store a map of input key values to action names.

To register an action, the method [i]registerAction(int, string)[/i] will be provided which stores the values in the dictionary. Each child Scene will have its own map so it can have different actions available.

image.caption: Input keys being registered in a Scene.

content: The [b]GameEngine[/b] class will handle the actual input key presses and construct an [b]Action[/b] to dispatch to the current scene. When a Key is pressed, the [b]GameEngine[/b] will ask the [b]Scene[/b] if it has an action name associated with the key's integer value. If the [b]Scene[/b] has an associated action registered, the [b]GameEngine[/b] will create an [b]Action[/b] instance with the correct NAME and TYPE.

image.caption: In this example, the GameEngine checks the current Scene for an action registered for the Key event and dispatches an Action.

content: Once the [b]Action[/b] is sent to the [b]Scene[/b], the [b]Scene[/b] performs the logic associated with the [b]Action[/b] without caring how it was generated.

image.caption: An example of a Scene's doAction() method implementation.

content: Many games have functionality to record gameplay. Now that Scenes don't care where an Action comes from, we can implement Replay files by storing Action strings along with the specific game frame at which they occurred. Then load this file into the GameEngine and feed actions to the Scene.

The Player Entity int he game is represented by MegaMan, which has several different Animations: Stand, Run, and Air. You must determine which state the player is currently in and assign the correct Animation.
The player moves with the following controls:
Left:  A key
Right: D key
Jump:  W key
Shoot: [Space] key
The player can move left, right, or shoot at any time during the game. This means the player can move left or right while in mid-air.
The player can only jump if it is standing on a tile.

If the jump key is held down, the player should nto continuously jump, but instead only jump once per button press. If the player lets go of the jump key mid-jump, they should immediately begin to fall.
If the player moves left or right, they should face that direction until the opposite direction has been pressed.
Bullets shot by the player travel in the direction they are facing.
The player collides with 'Tile' entities in the level and cannot move through them. The player lands on a TIle entity and stands in place if it falls on them from above.
The player does not collide with 'Decorator' entities in the level.
If the player falls below the bottom of the screen, they respawn at the start
The player should have a Gravity component which constantly accelerates it downward on the screen until it collides with a tile.
The player has a maximum speed specified in the Level file which should not be exceeded in the x- or y-axis.
The player's sprite and bounding box are centered on the player's position.
Animations are implemented by storing multiple frames inside a texture.
The Animation class handles frame advancement based on animation speed
You need to implement Animation::update() to properly progress animations
You need to implement Animation::hasEnded() which returns true if animation has finished its last frame; false otherwise
Animations can be repeating (loop forever) or non-repeating (play once)
Any entity with a non-repeating animation should be destroyed once its Animation's hasEnded() returns true
Decoration entities are drawn to the screen and have no interaction with any other entities in the game in any way
Decorations can be given an animation, but intuitively they should be reserved for static things like clouds, bushes, etc.
Tiles are entities that define the level geometry and interact with players.
Tiles can be given an animation that is defined in the Assets file.
Tiles will be given a bounding box equal to the size of their animation. tile->getComponent<Animation>().animation.getSize()
The current animation for a tile can be retrieved with: tile->getComponent<Animation>().animation.getName()
Tiles have different behavior depending on the Animation they are given.
Brick tiles are given the 'Brick' animation
When a brick tile collides with a bullet or if the player hits it from below:
Its animation should change to 'Explosion' non-repeat
Non-repeating animation entities are destroyed when hasEnded() is true
Its BoundingBox component gets removed
Question tiles are given the 'Question' animation when created
When a Question tile collides with a player hitting from below:
Its animation should change to 'Question2'
A temporary lifespan entity with the 'Coin' animation should appear for 30 frames, 64 pixels above the location of the Question tile
Should stay the same
The 'P' key should pause the game
The 'T' key should toggle drawing textures
The 'C' key should toggle drawing bounding boxes of entities
The 'G' key should toggle drawing of the grid
The 'Esc' key should go back to the Main Menu or quit the game

content: The player will have a Gravity component that is an acceleration of velocity applied in the y-axis. This would be applied after in the Movement system, but after processing player movement (such as a jump). Try an initial gravity of 0.1. Velocity from Gravity should accelerate each frame until collision or reaching max speed.

Implement Gravity do that the player falls toward the bottom of the screen and lands on tiles when it collides with a tile from above. When the player stops due to a collision, you should set its y-velocity to 0 so it stops accelerating downwards.
